cleaned_entries.title: Recommended Terraform project structure
cleaned_entries.content:
Recommended Terraform project structure

Organize Terraform projects with separate files: main.tf (resources), variables.tf (input declarations), outputs.tf (outputs), providers.tf (provider config), versions.tf (version constraints), locals.tf (computed locals), and a modules/ directory for reusable components.

Decision rules:
- Separate concerns into dedicated files — do not put everything in main.tf
- Place reusable infrastructure patterns in modules/ with their own variables.tf and outputs.tf

Trade-offs:
- More files increase organization but require tooling (terragrunt, workspaces) for multi-environment management

Anti-patterns:
- Putting all resources, variables, and outputs into a single main.tf
- Hardcoding environment-specific values inside resource definitions

cleaned_entries.title: Secure remote state with S3 + DynamoDB backend
cleaned_entries.content:
Secure remote state with S3 + DynamoDB backend

Configure Terraform backend with S3 (encrypted, KMS key) and DynamoDB for state locking. Required fields: bucket, key, region, encrypt=true, kms_key_id, dynamodb_table. Prevents concurrent state modifications and encrypts sensitive state data at rest.

Decision rules:
- Always use a remote backend for team environments — never rely on local state
- Enable encrypt=true and provide a KMS key for state file encryption at rest
- Use DynamoDB for state locking to prevent concurrent terraform apply conflicts

Trade-offs:
- S3 backend requires the bucket and DynamoDB table to be provisioned before running terraform init

Anti-patterns:
- Committing terraform.tfstate files to version control — state may contain plaintext secrets
- Using local backend for shared or production environments

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- S3 bucket for state should have versioning enabled and public access blocked
- Use a dedicated AWS account for Terraform state storage

cleaned_entries.title: Handling sensitive variables in Terraform
cleaned_entries.content:
Handling sensitive variables in Terraform

Mark sensitive variables with sensitive = true to suppress their values in plan/apply logs. Never set sensitive defaults. Inject real values at runtime via environment variables: export TF_VAR_db_password=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value ...).

Decision rules:
- Add sensitive = true to any variable containing a password, token, or key
- Inject secrets via TF_VAR_* environment variables populated from a secrets manager at CI/CD time
- Never set a default value on a sensitive variable

Trade-offs:
- sensitive = true hides values in plan output but they are still stored in state — encrypt state

Anti-patterns:
- variable "db_password" { default = "mysecretpassword" }
- Passing secrets as CLI arguments (visible in shell history and process list)

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Retrieve secrets from AWS Secrets Manager in CI/CD before running Terraform apply

cleaned_entries.title: Secure Terraform output declarations
cleaned_entries.content:
Secure Terraform output declarations

Mark outputs that expose sensitive values with sensitive = true. Non-sensitive outputs (e.g. DB endpoint) can be marked sensitive = false. Sensitive outputs are still stored in state — ensure state is encrypted.

Decision rules:
- Set sensitive = true on any output that references a password, token, private key, or secret value
- Use outputs only for values required by other modules or CI/CD steps

Trade-offs:
- sensitive = true prevents outputs from being displayed but does not prevent them from being read by a caller module

Anti-patterns:
- Outputting raw DB passwords or private keys without sensitive = true
- Exporting secrets via outputs when they can be referenced directly within the same module

cleaned_entries.title: VPC with private and public subnets
cleaned_entries.content:
VPC with private and public subnets

Structure VPC with three layers: public subnets (ALB only, map_public_ip_on_launch=false), private app subnets (ECS/EKS workloads), private data subnets (RDS). Use count and cidrsubnet() for multi-AZ subnet creation. Apply common tags via local.common_tags.

Decision rules:
- Never assign public IPs to application or database instances — use private subnets
- Use at least 2 availability zones for high availability
- Set map_public_ip_on_launch=false even on public subnets — assign EIPs explicitly where needed

Trade-offs:
- NAT Gateway required for private subnet internet egress — adds cost (~$35/month per AZ)

Anti-patterns:
- Placing RDS instances in public subnets
- Using a single availability zone for production VPC

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use aws_nat_gateway in public subnets for outbound internet access from private subnets
- Use VPC Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB to avoid NAT Gateway costs for AWS API traffic

cleaned_entries.title: Restrictive security group configuration
cleaned_entries.content:
Restrictive security group configuration

Security groups should allow only required ingress traffic from specific sources (other SGs, not CIDRs where possible). Egress should be restricted to required protocols/ports. Never allow 0.0.0.0/0 ingress on ports 22 (SSH) or 3306 (MySQL). Add description to every rule.

Decision rules:
- Reference other security groups (not CIDR blocks) for ingress between AWS services
- Restrict egress to HTTPS (443) for services that only call external APIs
- Add a description field to every ingress/egress rule for auditability

Trade-offs:
- SG-to-SG references are region-specific — cross-region traffic requires CIDR-based rules

Anti-patterns:
- ingress from_port=22 cidr_blocks=["0.0.0.0/0"] — exposes SSH to the internet
- egress from_port=0 to_port=0 protocol=-1 cidr_blocks=["0.0.0.0/0"] — allows all outbound traffic

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Enable VPC Flow Logs to audit security group traffic
- Use AWS Config rule restricted-ssh to detect open SSH rules

cleaned_entries.title: IaC security scanning with tfsec and Checkov
cleaned_entries.content:
IaC security scanning with tfsec and Checkov

Integrate IaC scanners into CI/CD: tfsec (tfsec . --severity HIGH), Checkov (checkov -d . --framework terraform --check CKV_AWS_*), Terrascan (terrascan scan -t terraform -d .). Use aquasecurity/tfsec-action in GitHub Actions workflows.

Decision rules:
- Run tfsec or Checkov in CI/CD and fail the pipeline on HIGH severity findings
- Use --check CKV_AWS_* to apply AWS-specific CIS benchmark checks with Checkov

Trade-offs:
- Scanners may produce false positives for intentional deviations — use .tfsec/config.yml or checkov skip annotations to document exceptions

Anti-patterns:
- Running terraform apply without IaC security scanning in CI/CD
- Suppressing all scanner warnings without documentation

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- AWS Security Hub integrates with Checkov results via SARIF format

cleaned_entries.title: Centralized tagging with locals
cleaned_entries.content:
Centralized tagging with locals

Define common_tags in locals.tf and apply via tags = local.common_tags on every resource. Standard tags: Environment, Project, ManagedBy (terraform), Owner, CostCenter. Use merge(local.common_tags, {...}) to add resource-specific tags.

Decision rules:
- Apply common_tags to every taggable AWS resource for cost allocation and governance
- Use merge() to extend common tags with resource-specific tags rather than duplicating the base set

Trade-offs:
- Tags are eventually consistent on some AWS services — not suitable for real-time access control

Anti-patterns:
- Hardcoding tag values individually on each resource instead of using locals
- Not tagging resources — prevents cost attribution and governance enforcement

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- AWS Cost Explorer and Cost Allocation Tags require consistent tagging
- AWS Config can enforce mandatory tags via required-tags managed rule

cleaned_entries.title: Use pinned versions for Terraform modules
cleaned_entries.content:
Use pinned versions for Terraform modules

Always pin module sources to a specific version when using Terraform Registry or Git sources. Example: module vpc with source terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws and version = "5.5.1". Never use "latest" or an unpinned source.

Decision rules:
- Pin module version to a specific release tag — never omit the version field
- Update module versions deliberately after reviewing the changelog for breaking changes

Trade-offs:
- Pinned versions require manual updates — use Dependabot for Terraform to automate version bump PRs

Anti-patterns:
- Omitting the version field on registry modules — pulls the latest version on every init
- Using a git branch reference (ref=main) instead of a tag — non-deterministic builds
